newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cyprus unity talks end in disarray.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus unity talks end in disarray.

text.p: U.N. talks aimed at breaking through decades of division in Cyprus ended in disarray on Friday with Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders wrangling in public.

But U.N. mediator and special Cyprus envoy Diego Cordovez, although exasperated after five days of fruitless talks under a media clampdown in an isolated hotel, put on a brave face on the lack of tangible progress and vowed to continue the process.
"The two leaders remain committed to achieving a settlement of the Cyprus problem. They held useful discussions. We will proceed on that basis," he told a closing news conference.
Cordovez said he accepted an invitation from both sides to visit the Mediterranean island at a future date and that talks would continue on humanitarian issues. But he had no date for a new round.

He said he would report on the talks to the U.N. Security Council in New York on Wednesday when he would also meet U.S. troubleshooter Richard Holbrooke, Washington`s result-oriented, forceful Cyprus envoy who brokered an end to the war in Bosnia.

Cordovez had been unable to get Glafcos Clerides, president of the internationally-recognised Greek Cypriot government in the south of the island, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash to agree to a compromise framework text.
The talks followed an inconclusive first round in New York in July and aimed at reuniting the island under a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.
Cypriot Greeks and Turks have been estranged since 1963 when a government in which both took part collapsed amid violence.
Turkey invaded the northern third in 1974 after a coup in the capital Nicosia engineered by the rightist junta then ruling Greece.

Although the two rival communities have been living in mostly peaceful separation throughout most of the long-running Cyprus problem, the post-1974 partition has led to an entrenching of positions with no sign of compromise.

However frustrating for the U.N. and other Western mediators, the inconclusive talks were business as usual for Denktash, 73, and Clerides, 78, old sparring partners who have held fruitless, hard-boiled negotiations for decades.
After the talks ended, the pair traded accusations through a marathon of separate news conferences as reporters rushed from one to another.
Clerides threatened to pull out of the talks if the EU delayed its plans to start entry talks for Cyprus early next year, while Denktash vowed to walk out if the plan went ahead.
On the last day alone, Cordovez put forward at least 10 drafts of a planned final U.N. statement which were vetoed in turn before he decided to give up.

"There were at least 10 different drafts of the statement which Mr Cordovez wanted to make. At least half of them Mr Denktash objected to and I objected to the other half," Clerides told his own news conference at Montreux Palais where the Greek Cypriot delegation in staying.
Clerides said: "Not only do I have no intention of delaying the (EU) process, but I must state that if there is any interference with it, I won`t be negotiating."

Across the road at the Intercontinental Hotel, Denktash put the blame on the Greek Cypriots for refusing to share power with the Turkish Cypriots and the EU for throwing in a "bombshell" in the talks by announcing plans to start entry talks for Cyprus early next year.

Denktash said: "I made no secret of the fact that we would not talk if the EU starts negotiating with Cyprus. The Greek Cypriot side which calls itself the government of Cyprus has been doing all it can to destroy our rights as co-founding partners."
Both men said the current session was doomed to failure from the first day but still appealed to the United Nations to keep the process going.
